lyrics:
Gentlemen, homeowners, debtors, sufferers—
I’ve brought back the thing you locked in the drawer after midnight

Tap-drip, tap-drip
Knee-tick, knee-tick
The guy who “forgot” the invoice again
sitting there like a bad splice
Car idling rough in the bayside cold
Bread not rising
There’s a little cure in the lacquered tray
You don’t need a lecture—
just something
to bite the edge

Drop-forged
Thumb-gripped
Polished for display
Everyone wants it
Nobody needs it anyway

KNURLED SPANNER
It looks like it knows your name
KNURLED SPANNER
Turns with a borrowed kind of grace
Loose wire
Bad timing
Phone on mute
Rent reminders
KNURLED SPANNER says, “I can probably help.”

(Probably help.)
(Probably help.)
No warranty on the mood

Mrs. Vale on Sycamore Close
Kept a rota by the sink
She bought three “sensible” lampshades
And still had time to think
Then she pinched the knurled handle
Just a quarter of a turn—
Now the tumble dryer hums like traffic
And her patience didn’t burn

Metric
Imperial
Domestic
Ceremonial

KNURLED SPANNER
It looks like it knows your name
KNURLED SPANNER
Turns with a borrowed kind of grace
Tax form
Bad karma
Loose hinge
Inner drama
KNURLED SPANNER says, “I can probably help.”

Please note
the knurling is mostly there
so your hand feels employed
while the thing itself
does very little

If your wedding starts to clatter
At eleven after ten
If your boss says, “Circle back”
For the fourth time, once again
If the bin men leave a note
In a font you can’t decode
Set your jaw like you mean business
And give the thing a load
Not on the bolt
On the story

That’s where most people get it wrong

KNURLED SPANNER
(What’s it for?)
Mostly looking useful in a tray
KNURLED SPANNER
(Does it work?)
When the problem wants to play
Hairline fracture
Paper capture
Cheap distraction
Tax subtraction
KNURLED SPANNER fixes that

Now, a few determined critics
have pointed out the knurled spanner
will not mend a voicemail you shouldn’t have heard
replace a missing week
settle the downstairs argument
or make the council act like adults
These critics
have clearly
confused “tool”
with “permission.”

Grip it
Show it
Set it down
Let the ugly little wheel go round
One more half-turn—
That feels profound

KNURLED SPANNER
It looks like it knows your name
KNURLED SPANNER
Turns with a borrowed kind of grace
Moral panic
Pipe organ panic
Fuel gauge
Pocket plague
KNURLED SPANNER fixes that

Headache
Spanner
Bad luck
Spanner
That thing you keep calling progress

You still don’t need it
And you never did

style: Progressive experimental rock/jazz fusion in 7/8, with electric-piano ostinato and clipped brass over dry talk-sung vocals, Two guitars trade angular, hard-rock riffs while interlocked bass and polyrhythmic drums pivot through shifting keys, Multi-keyboards, marimba, and flute add surreal color; abrupt classical ensemble cuts freeze the momentum.

  Approved critic summary: For a songwriter introduced as a diarist, a philosopher of the ordinary who finds a lifetime in a reflection on a phone screen, "Outlandia" is a startling pivot: a two-hour rock opera, twenty-four scenes long, about how a country is bought, broken, and inventoried.

  Approved critic summary: After the two-hour sprawl of "Outlandia," Rose narrows the lens back down to something you can hold in one hand, and "Them Bones" benefits from the compression.

review.review_text: The pitch arrives like a late-night infomercial run through a jazz-fusion band that refuses to sit still: an electric-piano ostinato loops in 3/4 at a brisk 136 while clipped brass and two guitars trade angular jabs, and Rose talk-sings the whole con with a straight face. The joke is right there in the object itself, a spanner whose knurling is "mostly there so your hand feels employed while the thing itself does very little," and Rose builds an entire satire of useless progress on that one image. Mrs. Vale on Sycamore Close gets her verse and her ruined tumble dryer; the mock-critic bridge lands the sharpest line of the record when it accuses us of confusing "tool" with "permission." The deadpan post-chorus, those flat "(Probably help.)" backing vocals with "no warranty on the mood," is the kind of detail that rewards a second pass. It runs a touch long across its five minutes, and the wiry guitar solo repeats its figure a beat past where you want it to move on, so this reads as one for listeners already tuned to Rose's dry wit rather than a first handshake. But the closing turn, the ostinato left alone and that final "You still don't need it, and you never did," gives the gag a real spine. A grower, and a smart one.
